title: Manage containers in Azure Container Apps

questions.q: You want to send 10% of traffic to a revision running a new model version and 90% to the current one. Which revision mode do you need?

options.text: Inactive revision mode
options.why: Inactive is a revision state, not a mode.

options.text: Multiple revision mode
options.why: Correct. Multiple revision mode enables canary rollouts and traffic splitting.

options.text: Labelled revision mode
options.why: Learn describes only single and multiple revision modes.

options.text: Single revision mode
options.why: Single revision mode keeps only one active revision, so you can't split traffic.

questions.hint: Sending a share of traffic to each of two revisions needs more than one active revision.
questions.explain: Multiple revision mode allows several active revisions, which enables traffic splitting.

questions.q: What does it mean when a Container Apps revision is active?

options.text: It has passed every health probe
options.why: Health and active state are separate properties.

options.text: It is in a state where it can receive traffic
options.why: Correct. Active is the operational state that lets a revision receive traffic.

options.text: It is the newest revision of the app
options.why: A newer revision can exist without being active.

options.text: It is stored with its image digest
options.why: Activity isn't tied to how the image is referenced.

questions.hint: A revision can exist without receiving traffic. What does the word active add?
questions.explain: A revision can exist without being active; only active revisions can receive traffic.

questions.q: A new revision starts returning errors in production. You want it to stop receiving traffic while keeping the evidence for later analysis. What should you do first?

options.text: Purge revisions with --max-inactive-revisions 0
options.why: Purging removes inactive revisions you may need.

options.text: Restart the whole container app
options.why: A restart doesn't stop traffic to that revision and doesn't isolate it.

options.text: Delete the revision so no new replicas start
options.why: Deletion destroys the evidence and the rollback option.

options.text: Deactivate the revision to stop its traffic
options.why: Correct. Deactivation stops traffic while preserving evidence and rollback options.

questions.hint: Stop the traffic but keep the evidence. Deleting removes evidence.
questions.explain: Deactivation is a safer first step than deletion during an incident.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team updates production with `az containerapp update --image myregistry.azurecr.io/ai-api@sha256:…`.

rows.text: Referencing the digest lets the team prove which artifact served requests during an incident.
rows.why: Digests are immutable, so they give strong traceability.

rows.text: Container Apps keeps every inactive revision forever unless someone deletes it.
rows.why: Inactive revisions are purged automatically when you exceed 100.

rows.text: The update creates a new revision with the updated template.
rows.why: Updating the image creates a new revision.

rows.text: A tag such as staging is a guarantee that the image content never changes.
rows.why: Tags can change; treat them as a convenience.

questions.hint: Digests prove which artifact ran. Think about what an image update creates and how inactive revisions are cleaned up.
questions.explain: Use digests in production, check the new revision's health, and know the 100-revision purge threshold.

questions.q: Your app uses the default single revision mode. You update the image, and the new revision becomes healthy. How many revisions can be active now?

options.text: Up to 100, after which inactive ones are purged
options.why: 100 is the default purge threshold for inactive revisions, not a limit on active ones.

options.text: Two, so that traffic can be split during the rollout
options.why: Traffic splitting needs multiple revision mode, which isn't the default.

options.text: One
options.why: Correct. Single revision mode keeps only one active revision.

options.text: As many as the app's maximum replica count
options.why: Replica limits count running instances. They don't decide how many revisions are active.

questions.hint: The mode's name tells you the answer.
questions.explain: Revision mode determines how many revisions can be active at once. Single revision mode keeps only one active revision; multiple revision mode allows canary rollouts and traffic splitting.

questions.q: You updated a production app to an image digest. Before routing traffic, you want to confirm the platform recorded exactly the image you expect. Which command shows it?

options.text: az containerapp logs show --type system
options.why: System logs show platform events. They don't list the configured image reference.

options.text: az containerapp env show --query properties.containers
options.why: Containers are defined in each app's template, not in the environment.

options.text: az acr repository show-manifests --name myregistry
options.why: That lists manifests in the registry, not what the container app is configured to run.

options.text: az containerapp show --query properties.template.containers
options.why: Correct. The container template shows the image reference the platform recorded.

questions.hint: The image reference lives in the app's template. Show the app and query that part.
questions.explain: After an update, inspect the container template with az containerapp show --query properties.template.containers to confirm the image you expect.

questions.q: Auditors want inactive revisions kept far longer than usual, so that up to 300 old revisions remain available for incident review. What should you change?

options.text: Raise --max-inactive-revisions above the default threshold of 100
options.why: Correct. Container Apps purges inactive revisions beyond 100 by default, and --max-inactive-revisions adjusts that threshold.

options.text: Switch the app to multiple revision mode so that inactive revisions are kept longer
options.why: Revision mode controls how many revisions are active. It doesn't change the purge threshold.

options.text: Deactivate each revision manually, since purging applies to deleted revisions
options.why: Deactivated revisions are exactly the inactive ones that the purge threshold applies to.

options.text: Tag each revision's image with a stable tag so that the platform keeps it
options.why: Image tags don't affect how many inactive revisions Container Apps keeps.

questions.hint: There's a default number of inactive revisions kept, and a parameter that changes it.
questions.explain: Container Apps automatically purges inactive revisions when you exceed 100. Adjust the threshold with --max-inactive-revisions as part of a retention strategy.

questions.q: Revision ai-api--v7 fails while ai-api--v6 works. You want to compare the two revisions' configuration side by side. Which command retrieves one revision's details?

options.text: az containerapp replica list --revision ai-api--v7
options.why: This lists running instances, not the revision's configuration.

options.text: az containerapp logs show --revision ai-api--v7 --follow
options.why: Logs show runtime output. Comparing configuration needs the revision's details.

options.text: az containerapp revision show --revision ai-api--v7
options.why: Correct. revision show returns a specific revision's details, so you can compare it with a working one.

options.text: az containerapp revision deactivate --revision ai-api--v7
options.why: Deactivation stops traffic to the revision. It doesn't show its configuration.

questions.hint: List shows all revisions. Which verb gives you the details of one?
questions.explain: Listing revisions confirms which is active; az containerapp revision show retrieves a specific revision so you can compare a working and a failing configuration.

questions.q: An upstream model provider is down, and you must guarantee that the app doesn't start any replicas until it's back. What should you do?

options.text: Rely on scale to zero
options.why: Scale to zero depends on scale rules; incoming work can still start replicas.

options.text: Run az containerapp stop
options.why: Correct. Stop is an explicit action that guarantees no replicas start.

options.text: Lower the CPU allocation
options.why: CPU size doesn't stop replicas from starting.

options.text: Run az containerapp restart
options.why: Restart starts replicas again.

questions.hint: Scaling rules can still start replicas. Which explicit action guarantees none start?
questions.explain: Stopping is an explicit operational action; scale to zero is automatic and can scale back out.

questions.q: Match each failing revision symptom to the checklist category.

items.text: Registry credentials are missing, so the revision never starts
items.why: Missing or invalid credentials or a wrong image reference cause pull failures.

items.text: The container listens on 5000 but ingress targets 8000
items.why: The container listens on a different port than ingress expects.

items.text: Readiness checks /healthz but the app serves /health
Replicas are killed while loading a large model
items.why: Containers killed at memory limits are resource pressure.

questions.hint: Each symptom points to one category: registry, port, probe or resources.
questions.explain: Learn's repeatable checklist: image pull, port, missing configuration, probes, resource pressure.

questions.q: Only the newest revision is failing; two older revisions in multiple revision mode are serving traffic fine. Which first step limits the blast radius best?

options.text: Restart the container app to clear the bad state
options.why: A restart affects the whole app and isn't a root-cause fix.

options.text: Stop the container app until the cause is known
options.why: Stop is app-level and would take the healthy revisions down too.

options.text: Delete the two older revisions to avoid confusion
options.why: The older revisions are healthy and are your rollback path.

options.text: Deactivate the failing revision and keep the others serving
options.why: Correct. Deactivating one revision isolates the bad release.

questions.hint: Only one revision is bad. App-level actions affect every revision.
questions.explain: Start, stop and restart act on the whole app. For one bad release, deactivate that revision.

questions.q: After a configuration change, you want the change to take effect immediately. You also suspect one replica is stuck in a deadlock. Which lifecycle action fits?

options.text: az containerapp stop
options.why: Stop keeps the app from starting replicas at all. It's for incidents, not for applying a change.

options.text: az containerapp revision deactivate
options.why: Deactivation removes a revision from traffic. It doesn't restart replicas.

options.text: az containerapp restart
options.why: Correct. Restart forces replicas to restart, which applies configuration immediately and can clear a stuck process.

options.text: Set the minimum replicas to zero and wait
options.why: Scale to zero depends on traffic and rules, so it doesn't apply a change right away.

questions.hint: You want running replicas to start again, not to disappear.
questions.explain: Restart is useful when configuration changes should take effect immediately, or when a process is stuck because of a deadlock or a transient dependency issue. Pair it with log inspection.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An AI API loads a large model at startup, and the on-call engineer often restarts it when latency rises.

rows.text: Frequent restarts can increase how often users hit cold starts.
rows.why: Each restart reloads the model, so restarting too aggressively increases cold starts.

rows.text: A restart that makes latency normal again proves the root cause is fixed.
rows.why: Restart isn't a substitute for root cause. Pair it with log inspection to see whether it fixed or delayed the failure.

rows.text: Stopping the app affects every revision, not only the one with problems.
rows.why: Start and stop are app-level actions, which can be too broad when one revision is the problem.

questions.hint: Think about what a restart costs a model-loading API, what it proves, and how wide stop reaches.
questions.explain: Restart clears transient states but isn't a root-cause fix, and frequent restarts increase cold starts for model-loading services. Start and stop are app-level, so revision deactivation is safer for one bad release.

questions.q: During an incident, you want one table that shows every revision's name, whether it's active, and its health state. Which command does Learn use as a starting point?

options.text: az containerapp logs show --type system --query revisions -o table
options.why: Logs are a stream of events, not a status table of revisions.

options.text: az containerapp show --query properties.template.revisions -o table
options.why: The app's template describes the current container definition, not every revision's status.

options.text: az containerapp revision list with --query "[].{name:name,active:properties.active,health:properties.healthState}" -o table
options.why: Correct. This query compares revision status at a glance.

options.text: az containerapp replica list --query "[].{name:name,health:properties.healthState}" -o table
options.why: Replicas are running instances. The question asks about revisions.

questions.hint: You're listing revisions and picking three fields with a JMESPath query.
questions.explain: Learn's checklist starts by confirming which revision is failing; az containerapp revision list with a --query for name, active and healthState compares revisions at a glance.

questions.q: Which two fields does Learn recommend adding to an AI API's application logs? (Select two.)

options.text: A request identifier propagated across services
options.why: Correct. A correlation ID ties logs together across services.

options.text: The full text of the user's prompt, for exact replay later
options.why: Log identifiers and metadata rather than prompts.

options.text: The model version used for the request
options.why: Correct. The model deployment name or version helps explain behavior.

options.text: The raw document that was processed, for later debugging
options.why: Avoid logging raw documents; they can be sensitive.

questions.hint: Two fields help you tie a request to the exact path and model that served it.
questions.explain: Recommended fields: request id, revision or build id, model version, latency breakdown.

questions.q: A new revision fails in production. Put Learn's incident workflow in order.
steps: Confirm which revision is active and which is failing
Stream logs while you reproduce the issue
Compare the configuration of a working and the failing revision
Apply a targeted fix and validate that the next revision becomes ready
questions.hint: Scope first, then watch, then compare, then fix and confirm.
questions.explain: Narrow the scope first, gather live evidence, compare configs, then fix and validate.

questions.q: Some prompts make the AI API fail, and developers want the logs to help debug them. Security forbids storing sensitive user content in logs. What should the API log?

options.text: Identifiers and metadata such as request ID and model version
options.why: Correct. Logging identifiers and metadata rather than raw prompts gives context without sensitive content.

options.text: The full prompt and response, encrypted with a key in Key Vault
options.why: Encryption still stores the sensitive content, which the guidance avoids.

options.text: HTTP status codes alone, so that no request detail is stored
options.why: Status codes alone don't give enough context to debug input-dependent failures.

options.text: The full prompt and response, but just for requests that fail
options.why: Failed requests can still contain sensitive content, so this still logs it.

questions.hint: You want enough context to trace a request without keeping what the user wrote.
questions.explain: AI services behave differently for different inputs. Log identifiers and metadata (request ID, revision or build ID, model version, latency breakdown) instead of raw documents or prompts.

questions.q: What happens when a liveness probe fails for a replica?

options.text: The revision is deactivated
options.why: Probes act on replicas, not on revision activation.

options.text: The replica stops receiving traffic but keeps running
options.why: That's the readiness behavior.

options.text: The platform restarts the replica
options.why: Correct. If liveness fails, the platform restarts the replica.

options.text: The app scales to zero
options.why: Probe failures don't trigger scale to zero.

questions.hint: One probe decides about traffic, and the other decides about restarts.
questions.explain: Readiness controls traffic; liveness controls restarts.

questions.q: An AI API loads a 3 GB model at startup. New revisions are restarted again and again by the liveness probe about 20 seconds after starting, before the model finishes loading. What should you change?

options.text: Raise initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to match the model load time
options.why: Correct. Tune these values so the process has enough time to reach a ready state.

options.text: Point the liveness probe at a downstream dependency's health URL
options.why: Probe endpoints shouldn't depend on external systems.

options.text: Remove the readiness probe so traffic reaches the replica sooner
options.why: Removing readiness sends traffic to replicas that can't serve it.

options.text: Restart the container app after each deployment
options.why: Restarts make the cold-start problem worse.

questions.hint: The probe fires before the model finishes loading. Give the process more time before failures count.
questions.explain: Liveness failures shortly after startup usually mean the probe is too aggressive for the real startup time.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A new revision fails its probes during rollout.

rows.text: Revision status shows whether the platform considers the revision healthy.
A probe failure is almost always a bug in the application code.
rows.why: Learn says probe failures are frequently configuration issues.

rows.text: A readiness endpoint that calls an external API can fail during that API's outage.
rows.why: Probe endpoints shouldn't depend on external systems that might be unavailable.

rows.text: Making liveness more aggressive reduces cold starts for model-heavy apps.
rows.why: Aggressive liveness causes unnecessary restarts and more cold starts.

questions.hint: Probe failures are often configuration. Revision status and dependency calls matter.
questions.explain: Check port, path, timeouts and startup dependencies first; tune probes to the real startup behavior.

questions.q: Each new replica of an AI API spends 40 seconds loading a model. During that time, requests that reach it fail. Which probe should protect users from this?

options.text: A readiness probe that succeeds only after the model is loaded
options.why: Correct. Readiness decides whether a replica can receive traffic, so it guards model loading.

options.text: A liveness probe on the same path as the readiness probe
options.why: Sharing a path doesn't stop traffic reaching an unready replica. That's readiness's job.

options.text: A liveness probe with a very short timeout
options.why: Liveness decides whether to restart a replica. A short timeout would cause restarts during loading.

options.text: A startup command that sleeps for 40 seconds
options.why: A sleep doesn't tell the platform when the replica can take traffic.

questions.hint: One probe asks "can this replica receive traffic right now?"
questions.explain: Readiness answers "Can this replica receive traffic right now?" If it fails, the platform stops routing to that replica. Use it to guard model loading and dependency readiness.

questions.q: A new revision's readiness probe calls /health/ready on port 80, but the API serves on port 8080. Logs show the API started normally. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Change the probe's port to 8080
options.why: Correct. A probe that targets the wrong port is one of the most common probe failures.

options.text: Remove the readiness probe so that traffic flows straight away
options.why: That sends traffic to replicas before you know they're ready.

options.text: Rewrite the /health/ready handler, because probe failures usually mean an application bug
options.why: Probe failures are frequently configuration issues. The app started normally.

options.text: Lower the liveness probe's failureThreshold to 1
options.why: That makes liveness more aggressive and doesn't fix the readiness probe's port.

questions.hint: The app is fine, and the probe is knocking on a door nobody is behind.
questions.explain: Common probe failure causes: wrong port, wrong path, timeouts too short for model loading, and slow or failing dependency calls at startup. Check configuration before chasing code.

questions.q: A background worker keeps restarting, and logs show out-of-memory kills while it processes large batches. What should you increase first?

options.text: CPU per replica
options.why: CPU addresses throttling, not out-of-memory restarts.

options.text: Memory per replica
options.why: Correct. Size for the bottleneck: memory for out-of-memory restarts.

options.text: Minimum replica count
options.why: More replicas don't give each replica more memory.

options.text: Maximum inactive revisions
options.why: Revision retention doesn't affect memory.

questions.hint: Out-of-memory kills point to one resource. Size for the bottleneck.
questions.explain: Increase CPU when you see throttling and memory when you see out-of-memory restarts.

questions.q: A synchronous chat API must avoid cold-start delays, and the team accepts a higher baseline cost. What should you configure?

options.text: A liveness probe with a lower threshold
options.why: An aggressive liveness probe causes more restarts.

options.text: Single revision mode for the app
options.why: Revision mode doesn't keep replicas warm.

options.text: Scale to zero with a short cooldown period
options.why: Scale to zero is what causes cold starts here.

options.text: A minimum replica count above zero
options.why: Correct. Minimum replicas reduce cold starts but increase baseline cost.

questions.hint: Cold starts are avoided by keeping replicas warm, at a cost.
questions.explain: Use minimum replicas intentionally: fewer cold starts, more baseline cost.

questions.q: After a model upgrade, p95 latency doubled. You plan to raise CPU, raise memory and change the replica limits. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Change the three settings together to fix the problem fastest
options.why: Several changes at once mask which one fixed it.

options.text: Roll back the model, since resource changes won't affect model latency
options.why: Learn says to reassess resources after model changes, not to rule them out.

options.text: Change one variable at a time and measure after each change
options.why: Correct. Optimization is iterative; change one variable at a time.

options.text: Set the minimum replicas equal to the maximum to take scaling out of the picture
options.why: Fixing replicas at the maximum just raises cost.

questions.hint: Several changes at once hide which one helped.
questions.explain: Use logs and metrics to find the bottleneck, then change one variable at a time.

questions.q: Under high concurrency, an AI API's latency spikes, and metrics show CPU throttling. Memory use is low, and there are no restarts. What should you change first?

options.text: Restart the app every hour
options.why: Restarts don't add CPU, and they add cold starts for a model-loading API.

options.text: Increase CPU per replica
options.why: Correct. Size for the bottleneck: increase CPU when you see throttling.

options.text: Set the minimum replicas to zero
options.why: Scale to zero adds cold starts and doesn't address throttling.

options.text: Increase memory per replica
options.why: Memory raises help with out-of-memory restarts, which aren't happening here.

questions.hint: Match the fix to the metric that's under pressure.
questions.explain: Size for the bottleneck: increase CPU when you see throttling, and increase memory when you see out-of-memory restarts. Validate that per-replica CPU supports your concurrency.

questions.q: An event-driven background worker summarizes documents a few times a day and can drain its work safely when it scales down. The team wants the lowest cost. How should you set its minimum replicas?

options.text: Keep at least one replica so that it never cold-starts
options.why: A minimum replica avoids cold starts but adds baseline cost, which this worker doesn't need.

options.text: Allow scale to zero
options.why: Correct. Event-driven workers that drain work safely can often tolerate scale to zero, which keeps the baseline cost low.

options.text: Set the minimum to two for redundancy
options.why: Two idle replicas raise baseline cost for work that only arrives a few times a day.

options.text: Match the minimum to the maximum so that capacity is fixed
options.why: Fixed capacity pays for idle replicas most of the day.

questions.hint: Compare a synchronous API, which needs warm replicas, with a worker whose work can wait.
questions.explain: A synchronous API often needs a minimum replica count to reduce cold starts. A background worker that's event-driven and drains work safely can often tolerate scale to zero.
